canonical_topic: Economy of scale in coal-fired generation shaped the grid
definition: Large, centralized coal-fired power plants are cheaper to operate per unit of output than small ones, and this economy of scale is a major reason the electrical grid developed around centralized generation with extensive transmission networks.
core_idea: Coal plant economics favor bigness, and that preference for scale is a structural driver behind the historical shape of the power grid (large centralized plants plus long transmission lines) rather than a distributed generation model.
key_points: Big, centralized coal plants are cheaper to run than small coal plants (economy of scale).
The grid's current architecture — centralized generation plus extensive transmission — is attributed in large part to this coal-driven economy of scale.
relationships: Links coal plant scale economics to overall grid/transmission architecture.
trading_implications: Understanding why the grid is centralized helps explain transmission constraints and locational price dynamics that persist even as generation mix shifts away from coal.
